description: We’re looking for creative, curious, and bold people who love to explore, learn, and go beyond what is expected. For us, Space Apps is more than just a competition—it’s an opportunity to learn, create, and challenge ourselves. We believe that with curiosity, courage, and a good team, there are no limits to what we can achieve.
summary:
When a space mission ends, its equipment does not lose its importance. Landers, rovers, scientific instruments and reflectors left on the Moon and Mars carry engineering, human and scientific stories that deserve to be remembered. However, these stories often remain inaccessible to young people because they are presented in technical archives.

After Mission is a mobile application that transforms young people aged 12 to 18 into space tourists. Each user receives a personal Space Passport, chooses a destination (the Moon or Mars), and selects a guide: a retired piece of NASA equipment that tells its story in the first person.

Through interactive levels, the guide shares real events, asks questions and presents choices. The tourist answers before discovering what actually happened, using real NASA data.

The project considers retired space equipment as monuments in space, representing important landmarks of human exploration. Each completed adventure earns the tourist a passport stamp and a personalised boarding pass, encouraging them to discover other monuments.

We chose this challenge because of its emotional dimension: giving a voice to abandoned equipment means recognising that nothing that served humanity deserves to be forgotten. Young people are the future of space exploration, and awakening their curiosity today can inspire tomorrow's innovators.
details:
1. Executive summary

When a space mission ends, the machine does not stop being interesting, and it must not be forgotten. A lander that carried people to another world, a laboratory that kept transmitting for weeks after its crew had gone, a reflector that is still on the Moon: each of them holds an engineering story, a human story and a scientific legacy. Yet for most young people, these stories stay locked inside technical archives.

After Mission is a mobile application that turns young people aged 12 to 18 into space tourists. Each tourist has a personal Space Passport, chooses a destination, the Moon or Mars, and then chooses a guide: a retired piece of NASA equipment that speaks in the first person. Level by level, the guide tells part of its real story, asks the tourist a question, listens to the answer, and then reveals what truly happened, using real data from NASA.

In After Mission, the equipment that NASA left on the Moon and Mars is considered as monuments in space: lasting landmarks of human exploration, worth visiting and worth protecting in memory, the way travelers visit the monuments of a country. When the adventure with one guide ends, the tourist receives a stamp in the passport and can travel on to the next monument, the way a traveler moves from one country to another. Every new stop adds to a growing collection, and to the tourist’s understanding of what humanity has left behind on the Moon and Mars.

We chose this challenge for its emotional strength: giving a voice to what is abandoned is a way of saying that nothing that served humanity deserves to be forgotten. Young people are the audience set by the concept of the challenge itself, and we embrace it fully: they are the future of space exploration, and a story that awakens their curiosity today can inspire the innovators of tomorrow.

Every fact in After Mission comes from the NASA open data made available during this hackathon. During the 48 hours of the hackathon we built the first stop of this journey: a complete, data-traceable story for Eagle, the Apollo 11 Lunar Module, together with the visual identity and the first application screens. Eagle is our proof of concept. The project itself is the platform: a repeatable way to give every retired machine a voice.

2. The challenge and the problem

The challenge asks teams to bring discarded and retired space equipment back to life through storytelling, and to help people understand the science behind it.

2.1 Why we chose this challenge

We chose “Abandoned but not Forgotten” first of all for its emotional side. Among all the challenges, this is the one that spoke to us on a human level. A lander left on the Moon, a rover that went silent on Mars: these machines were built by people, carried the hopes of whole nations, and ended their mission far from home. The title itself carries a promise that we wanted to keep: being abandoned does not mean being forgotten.

This emotional dimension is the heart of our approach. We do not want a young person to simply learn a date or a mass. We want them to feel something for a machine that finished its mission decades ago, to care about what happened to it, and to remember it. Emotion is what turns information into memory, and memory is exactly what keeps these stories alive.

2.2 Why young people

The target audience was not chosen by our team: it comes from the concept of the challenge itself, which places young people at its center. We share that conviction, because young people hold the future. The engineers, scientists and explorers who will design the next missions are today’s 12 to 18 year olds. If we awaken their curiosity now, we help build the generation that will develop the technologies, features and discoveries of tomorrow’s space exploration.

Curiosity is the first step. A teenager who falls in love with the story of Eagle may ask how a lunar module is built, how an engine is controlled during a descent, or what is still sitting on the Moon today. These questions can become school projects, studies and careers. After Mission aims to be the spark that starts that chain.

2.3 The gaps we identified

We identified three gaps that keep these stories from reaching young people.

Accessibility. Mission data exists as masses, timelines and frequencies. It is accurate, but it is not written for a teenager.

Passivity. Most space history is read or watched. Young learners retain more when they take part and make decisions.

Forgetting. Equipment that has stopped working fades from public attention, even though it carries lessons about engineering, risk and discovery.

Our guiding question is therefore: how can we make a young person care about a machine that finished its mission decades ago, while keeping every fact accurate?

3. Our idea: space tourism, with the equipment as guide

After Mission rests on one idea: every piece of space equipment has a story worth discovering, and it should tell that story itself. To make this experience feel like an adventure and not like a lesson, we frame it as space tourism.

3.1 The tourist and the Space Passport

The user signs in and becomes a space tourist. At sign-up the tourist receives a Space Passport, inspired by travel passports. The passport is the tourist’s identity in the application and also the record of the journey: it keeps the stamps earned along the way.

3.2 Two destinations

The tourist first chooses a destination, the Moon or Mars. Each destination presents the equipment that NASA left there. In this prototype the Moon is the destination we developed.

3.3 The equipment becomes the guide

On each destination, every piece of equipment is a character, not an entry in a catalogue. The tourist chooses one of them as a guide, and that guide accompanies the tourist through its whole story. The guide speaks in short, first-person turns, with its own voice, and welcomes the tourist as a traveler joining its mission.

In the experience, this equipment is considered as monuments in space. Eagle’s descent stage at Tranquility Base, a rover parked on the Martian plain, a reflector still facing Earth: each one stands where it was left, like a monument standing where history happened. The tourist is not browsing old machines, but visiting the landmarks of human exploration, the first monuments built by humanity beyond Earth, and each guide is the keeper of its own monument.

The model works for any equipment NASA has left behind. On the Moon, possible guides include the Apollo lunar modules, the lunar rovers, the Apollo science packages and the Surveyor landers. On Mars, they include the Viking landers, the Sojourner rover and the rovers Spirit and Opportunity. These examples show the scope we have in mind; the final selection will be made from NASA’s records.

3.4 A conversation, level by level

The heart of the experience is a conversation that moves forward one level at a time. Every level follows the same loop:

1. The guide tells. A short piece of its real story, with something at stake.

2. The guide asks. A question, or a decision that the tourist must make.

3. The tourist answers. The tourist chooses among plausible options.

4. The guide reacts. A short reaction in character to the choice made.

5. The guide reveals. What really happened, with real times, masses and distances.

Learning is therefore part of the adventure and not a quiz that follows it. The tourist is never simply told a fact: the tourist first commits to a guess, and the reveal answers a question the tourist has already asked themselves.

3.5 The Identification Card

Alongside the story, every piece of equipment has an Identification Card: a one-screen scientific reference with its main data (name, mission, dates, masses, dimensions, fate) and its data source. The story attracts the tourist; the card informs. Storytelling never replaces precise information.

3.6 From one story to the next: the passport as a journey

The Space Passport is what turns separate stories into one journey. When a tourist finishes the adventure with a guide, the passport receives a stamp for that piece of equipment, much like a traveler’s passport receives a stamp in each country visited. The tourist also keeps a personalised boarding pass as a souvenir of that stop.

The tourist can then choose another guide on the same destination, or travel to the other one. The Moon and Mars become two regions to explore, and each retired machine becomes a monument worth visiting. The more stamps the passport holds, the more of the story of space exploration the tourist has lived. This gives a sense of progression, a personal souvenir, and a natural reason to come back for the next adventure.

4. Target audience

The target audience of After Mission comes from the concept of the challenge itself: young people. After Mission addresses young people between 12 and 18 years old who are curious about space, from middle school to the end of high school. These are the future scientists, engineers and explorers of the space sector, and they are at the age where curiosity decides a path. This audience enjoys video games, animations and documentaries, discovers space content on platforms such as YouTube, and loses interest quickly in long, technical texts.

We represent this audience with a persona, Raid Adam, 14 years old, a middle-school student and space enthusiast. In his words:

“I want to discover the adventures of the robots sent into space, not just read facts about them!”

His needs shaped the project. Technical information must be explained in plain language, so the equipment speaks in short, first-person turns. History must not feel boring, so each story has something at stake, such as a landing with only one attempt. Websites feel passive to him, so every stop asks for a choice. Long texts lose his attention, so interaction replaces reading. And he wants accurate information, so every fact comes from NASA data and is labelled when it is calculated.

The persona is a design tool based on our understanding of the audience. Testing with real students aged 12 to 18 is part of our roadmap.

5. The user journey

The tourist moves through the application in seven steps:

1. Sign in. The tourist opens After Mission, signs in and receives a Space Passport. In our prototype, the example tourist is Raid Adam.

2. Choose a destination. The Moon or Mars.

3. Choose a guide. The equipment of that destination, its monuments in space, appears as a list of characters.

4. Meet the guide. The guide introduces itself, its crew and its mission, and welcomes the tourist.

5. Live the mission. Level by level, the tourist listens, answers and discovers the real history. Short optional side questions let curious users go deeper.

6. Keep the souvenir. The guide’s farewell, a personalised boarding pass and a stamp in the Space Passport.

7. Travel on. The tourist chooses the next guide, on the same destination or on the other one.

6. The prototype: Eagle, our first stop

A hackathon lasts 48 hours, so we did not build the full application. We built the first stop of the journey, to prove that the idea works end to end on one real piece of equipment. We chose Eagle, the Apollo 11 Lunar Module, whose mission has a complete public record in NASA’s open data.

The prototype follows Eagle’s real timeline, from its separation from the Command and Service Module to its release into lunar orbit: 30 hours and 17 minutes of history, told in five acts and nine interactive stops. At each stop the tourist makes a decision (as Collins at the separation, as the pilot during the descent, as an astronaut setting up the science package on the surface), and Eagle then reveals what actually happened.

For example, during the descent Eagle asks: “Fourteen and a half kilometers, Raid. It’s 20:05. How long does my engine stay lit?” The tourist chooses between about a minute, about twelve and a half minutes, or about half an hour. Each choice receives a short reaction in character. Eagle then reveals the truth: 756.3 seconds. Then Armstrong said: ‘Houston, Tranquility Base here, the Eagle has landed.’

What matters for the project is not only Eagle’s story, but the method behind it. Every new guide can be built in the same five steps:

1. Select a piece of equipment and its official NASA record.

2. Extract the facts from the NASA open data, and mark every value that is calculated rather than reported.

3. Write the story as a sequence of stops, each with a decision, plausible answer options and a reveal of the true event.

4. Create the Identification Card, with its data source.

5. Define the stamp and the souvenir that the tourist earns at the end.

This is what makes the idea scalable: once the method is set, each new piece of equipment on the Moon or Mars becomes one more monument on the tourist’s journey, without changing the structure of the experience.

Interactive UI/UX prototype and glassmorphism screen flows built in Figma.

7. Scientific accuracy

Storytelling must never cost accuracy. The guide’s personality shapes how things are said, never what happened.

7.1 NASA open data at the core of the project

After Mission is built on the NASA open data made available during this hackathon. This data is the foundation of the whole project: it is what allows us to tell real stories instead of invented ones. Every time, distance, mass and event told by a guide comes from NASA’s official records, and each story is built by reading, extracting and cross-checking that data. Open data is also what makes our method repeatable: any team, school or student can start from the same public records and give another machine a voice.

7.2 Our rules

• One source of facts. Each story is built from NASA’s official record of the equipment. For Eagle, this is the NASA National Space Science Data Center record of the Apollo 11 Lunar Module (ID 1969-059C), verified against NASA’s Apollo 11 documentation.

• Traceability. Every scene is mapped to the data it uses.

• Calculated values are labelled. Durations and masses derived from reported values are never presented as raw data.

• Wrong options are clearly fiction. The records describe what happened, not what was ruled out. The wrong answer options are plausible alternatives, and the reveal always states the true event.

• Unknowns stay unknown. When NASA does not know something, the guide says so. For example, the fate of Eagle’s ascent stage is told as unknown, never as fact.

8. Alignment with the judging criteria

Relevance. The challenge asks for storytelling about discarded equipment, on the Moon and Mars. After Mission makes the equipment itself the narrator and the guide, treats it as monuments in space, and offers both destinations as the two regions of one journey. Its emotional core answers the challenge’s own promise: abandoned, but not forgotten.

Creativity. Personified equipment, a space-tourism framing and a passport that records a journey from one monument to the next give an original structure to historical content. The story does not stop at facts: it asks the tourist to take part in the decisions that mattered.

Impact. The project addresses the young audience set by the challenge, teenagers who disengage from dense factual content, and who will shape the future of space exploration. The format applies to any equipment, so every new story strengthens the same educational platform and gives the tourist a reason to continue.

Validity. Content is traceable to the NASA open data of this hackathon. Calculated values are labelled, wrong options are identified as fiction, and unknowns are acknowledged.

Presentation. A consistent identity (logo, palette and slogan), a defined audience and persona, designed application screens, an Identification Card for each guide, a Space Passport, and a story with a clear beginning, real decisions and an emotional ending.

9. Team and conclusion

After Mission was created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Tangier by Ibtissam Ainzura, Samia Aoulad Hmidou and Imane El Assioui.

Space equipment does not stop being interesting when it stops working. Eagle’s descent stage still sits at Tranquility Base, and its ascent stage disappeared into mystery. These monuments in space and their stories belong to everyone, and a young person should be able to live them, not only read about them. After Mission gives each retired machine a voice, gives the tourist real decisions to make, and gives science a story to travel with.

Abandoned does not mean forgotten, and the young people who discover these stories today are the ones who will build tomorrow’s missions.

When the mission ends, the story lives on.
